screens.title: Why use Roles?
screens.narratorSegment: Roles are an organizational pattern in Ansible that group all artifacts related to a single concern into a predictable structure. That single claim hides important practical consequences. Reusability means you can write a role once, then share it across teams or projects. For example, a role that installs and configures Nginx becomes a single source of truth for that service; you do not copy tasks into every playbook. Modularity helps break large, monolithic playbooks into focused parts: one role for the webserver, another for the database, another for application deployment. This separation reduces cognitive load when you read or debug automation. Maintainability improves because a newcomer can look in the role's defaults, tasks, and templates to find where behavior is defined. Roles also encourage best practices: using defaults for overridable options, using handlers for service restarts, and packaging metadata in meta/main. yml. A common misconception is that roles add unnecessary complexity for small projects. In truth, even small but repeated automation benefits from a role. Begin by identifying repeated task groups — each becomes a good candidate for a role. As a takeaway, treat roles as reusable modules that make automation easier to version, test, and share.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Why use Roles?

Definition

A role packages all elements needed to perform a function into a standard directory layout so it can be reused and shared.

Reusability: Share my_nginx_role across projects instead of copying tasks.
Modularity: Keep one responsibility per role to simplify changes and testing.
Maintainability: Standard layout makes it easy for others to find logic and defaults.

Concrete example

Imagine Nginx installation repeated in three playbooks. Create a my_nginx_role with tasks to install, a template for nginx.conf using a variable for port, handlers to restart the service, and defaults for nginx_port. Apply the role in each playbook instead of duplicating tasks.
Key Takeaway

Roles are modular units that make automation consistent, reusable, and easier to maintain.

screens.title: Standard Role Directory Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A role follows a predictable directory layout that tells Ansible where to find each type of content. The most common directories are tasks, handlers, defaults, vars, templates, files, meta, and a README. Tasks/main. yml is the entry point executed when the role runs. Handlers/main. yml lists service restart or reload handlers you trigger with notify. Defaults/main. yml holds default values with the lowest precedence; they provide sensible settings users can override. Vars/main. yml contains role-specific high precedence variables used rarely and less likely to be overridden. Templates holds Jinja2 files used with the template module; these allow dynamic configuration by referencing role and inventory variables. Files holds static files to copy with the copy module. Meta/main. yml contains metadata such as author, license, and role dependencies that help composition. This layout matters because Ansible automatically searches these directories for relative src paths, so tasks can refer to a template simply by name. A common mistake is placing a template in the wrong directory or expecting the copy module to look in templates. Use this structure to make role content discoverable and portable.

keyIdea.text: Each role folder has a clear purpose: tasks run, handlers react, defaults are overridable, templates are dynamic, and files are static.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Role Directory Structure

Role folder map

my_role/
├── defaults/        # default variables
│   └── main.yml
├── handlers/        # restart/reload handlers
│   └── main.yml
├── tasks/           # main role tasks
│   └── main.yml
├── templates/       # Jinja2 templates
├── files/           # static files
├── vars/            # higher-precedence variables
│   └── main.yml
├── meta/            # metadata and dependencies
│   └── main.yml
└── README.md

Why the layout matters

  • Automatic lookup: template and file src paths are resolved inside the role.
  • Clear precedence: defaults vs vars defines which values are easy to override.
  • Separation of concerns: tasks do the work, handlers react to changes, templates render configs.
Misconception: You must use all folders. Reality: Use only the folders needed, but follow the convention when you do.

screens.title: tasks/main.yml — Role Entry Point
screens.narratorSegment: The tasks/main. yml file is the entry point Ansible reads when a role runs. It is the sequence of steps that implement the role's core behavior. You will often organize this file into includes or blocks to keep it readable, but at its simplest it lists tasks in order: install packages, deploy configuration templates, copy static files, and ensure services are running. Importantly, when a task makes a change to a configuration file, it should notify a handler rather than restart a service immediately. This ensures restarts happen only when necessary. A concrete example: first install the nginx package with the dnf module, then template the nginx configuration and notify "Restart Nginx", then ensure the nginx service is enabled and started. A common mistake is placing idempotent logic in a way that always reports changed, causing unnecessary restarts. Use modules and check options that preserve idempotence. As a quick practice, open tasks/main. yml and write a small sequence: package install, template deploy with notify, service ensure. That pattern will be reused across many roles. tasks/main.yml — Role Entry Point means list the core steps in tasks/main.yml and rely on handlers for reactive operations when changes occur.. In practical terms, how the role executes its tasks and triggers behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tasks drive the role
keyIdea.text: List the core steps in tasks/main.yml and rely on handlers for reactive operations when changes occur.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › tasks/main.yml

Code example

---
- name: Install Nginx package
  ansible.builtin.dnf:
    name: nginx
    state: latest

- name: Deploy Nginx configuration
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: '0644'
  notify: Restart Nginx

- name: Ensure Nginx is running and enabled
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: yes

Explanation & tips

  • Idempotence: Use modules that only report changed when needed to avoid spurious handler runs.
  • Notify pattern: Template changes should notify handlers instead of immediate restarts.
  • Order matters: Install packages before templating files that require binaries.
Example misconception: Running service restart immediately after a template may restart even if the file did not change. Use notify to restart only on change.

screens.title: Handlers and notify Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Handlers are special tasks that run only when notified by another task during the play. They are typically used to restart or reload services after a configuration change. The core idea is reactive control: a template or file task notifies a named handler when it reports changed, then handlers execute at the end of the role or play to apply required service actions. This reduces noise by ensuring restarts happen only when necessary. A simple flow: a template task writes a new config and reports changed; it sends notify: Restart Nginx; after the current host's tasks finish, Ansible runs the Restart Nginx handler. If multiple tasks notify the same handler, the handler runs just once. Common mistakes include forgetting to notify the handler, which leaves services running old configs, or naming mismatches between notify and handler names. Handlers can be defined inside the role so they are available when the role runs, or in the playbook level for cross-role handlers. Use clear handler names and keep them idempotent. As a final thought, think of handlers as event listeners that trigger only when a change event occurs.

keyIdea.text: Use notify to trigger handlers only on actual changes, minimizing unnecessary service restarts and ensuring predictable behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Handlers & notify

Handler example

# handlers/main.yml
---
- name: Restart Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
The template task uses notify: Restart Nginx. If the template reports changed, Ansible queues the handler. At the end of the role's tasks the handler runs once, even if multiple tasks notified it.

Process steps

1. Task runs and changes state
2. Task notifies handler name
3. Handler runs at end of host's tasks
Misconception: Handlers run immediately. They don't — they run after the current set of tasks for that host completes, which helps batch multiple changes to a single restart.

screens.title: defaults vs vars — Variable Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding variable precedence is essential when designing roles. defaults/main. yml contains default variables with the lowest precedence. They are ideal for providing sensible default settings that administrators can override through inventory, group_vars, host_vars, playbook vars, or extra vars. For example, put nginx_port: 80 in defaults so an inventory file can override it for a staging or production environment. Vars/main. yml has higher precedence than defaults; variables here are considered integral to the role and less likely to be overridden. Use vars for values that the role expects to remain constant or that should not be casually changed. A common mistake is placing environment-specific secrets in defaults — those should live in group_vars or be provided via Ansible Vault and inventory. Another pitfall is expecting defaults to block overrides; defaults are intentionally low precedence so they remain easy to override. When writing tasks and templates, reference variables without assuming where they come from, and document overridable settings in the role README. The guiding rule: defaults for flexible settings, vars for role-internal constants, and inventory for environment-specific values. defaults vs vars — Variable Precedence means put adjustable settings in defaults; put role-internal constants in vars; use inventory or vault for environment-specific secrets.. In practical terms, where to define configurable defaults and internal role variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › defaults vs vars

defaults/main.yml

# defaults/main.yml
nginx_port: 80
log_level: notice
Lowest precedence so administrators can override values in inventory or extra vars. Use for sensible defaults.

vars/main.yml

# vars/main.yml
internal_template_path: '/opt/role/templates'
service_user: nginx
Higher precedence. Use for role-internal values that should not be casually overridden.
Misconception: defaults are hidden. They are purposely low precedence to make roles flexible. For secrets, prefer inventory with Ansible Vault rather than defaults.

screens.title: Using files/ and templates/
screens.narratorSegment: Templates and files are how roles place content on managed hosts. Use the files/ directory for static files that do not require variable substitution, such as a static binary or a default index. html. Use templates/ for Jinja2 templates that render configuration dynamically based on variables. The template module will render templates and place the result on the target host, while the copy module uses files/ for direct copies. A key convenience of roles is that you do not need to specify full paths in src when calling template or copy: Ansible automatically searches the role's templates/ and files/ directories. For example, a template task with src: nginx. conf. j2 will find my_role/templates/nginx. conf. j2. Watch for the common error of putting a template in files/ and then expecting template to render it. Also avoid using absolute local paths which break portability. Use ownership, group, and mode settings in the task to ensure correct permissions. When you need dynamic configurations — for instance, inserting the nginx_port variable into an nginx. conf — templates are the correct choice. Using files/ and templates/ means place jinja2 templates in templates/ for variable-driven configs and static assets in files/ for copy tasks.. In practical terms, static files vs jinja2 templates and how to reference them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › files/ and templates/

Template example (nginx.conf.j2)

# server block using variable
server {
    listen       {{ nginx_port }};
    server_name  localhost;

    location / {
        root   /usr/share/nginx/html;
        index  index.html index.htm;
    }
}

Static file example

# files/default_index.html
<html>
  <body>Hello from my role</body>
</html>
Remember: template module renders Jinja2 with variables, copy module uses files/. Reference src by name inside role folders so tasks remain portable.

screens.title: meta/main.yml and Role Metadata
screens.narratorSegment: The meta/main. yml file holds metadata about the role such as author, supported platforms, license, and dependencies on other roles. Metadata helps automation consumers understand expectations and compatibility. For example, if a role depends on a common 'users' role to create accounts before services run, declare that dependency in meta/main. yml so ansible-galaxy or role import logic can install or run dependent roles in the correct order. Metadata also assists with discoverability when publishing roles to Ansible Galaxy. A small but useful practice is to include a short README. md that explains the role's purpose, available variables, default values, and any setup steps. This reduces onboarding time for other team members and reduces misconfiguration. screens.title: Apply Roles from a Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating roles into a playbook makes the playbook concise and focused on targets and orchestration. Instead of enumerating tasks, use roles: to apply one or more roles to the targeted hosts. A simple example playbook deploys a web role to the webservers group and lets the role own its internals. When the playbook runs, Ansible executes tasks/main. yml from the role, loads defaults and vars, and makes templates and files available via relative src names. Applying roles this way scales well as you add more roles to the same play; the playbook becomes an intent document rather than an implementation script. screens.title: Mistakes to Avoid and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes engineers make when adopting roles. First, variable precedence confusion: placing important environment-specific values in defaults/main. yml means they can be easily overridden, which is correct for tunable settings but wrong for secrets — those should be provided in group_vars, host_vars, or via Ansible Vault. Second, incorrect paths: a common error is using absolute or external paths for src in template or copy tasks. Remember that Ansible looks inside the role's templates/ and files/ directories by default, so use src: nginx. conf. j2 rather than a path to the role directory. Third, forgetting to notify handlers: if a template changes but no notify is present, the service will not reload and configuration changes will be useless until a manual restart. Fourth, always check idempotence — tasks that always report changed will trigger handlers repeatedly and cause unnecessary restarts. When troubleshooting, inspect task output to see which task returned changed and whether handlers were queued. Use smaller test playbooks targeting localhost to iterate quickly. These checks reduce debugging time and prevent unexpected downtime. Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Activity: Nginx role

deploy_web.yml

---
- name: Deploy Nginx web server using a role
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  roles:
    - nginx_webserver

defaults/main.yml

nginx_port: 80

tasks/main.yml & handlers

# tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Install Nginx package
  ansible.builtin.dnf:
    name: nginx
    state: latest

- name: Copy Nginx configuration template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: '0644'
  notify: Restart Nginx

- name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: yes

# handlers/main.yml
---
- name: Restart Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
Verification: Run ansible-playbook deploy_web.yml, then check the host with system tools to confirm nginx is installed, running, and listening on the expected port. Override nginx_port in group_vars to test different environments without changing the role itself.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn why Ansible roles are the right way to structure automation as your playbooks grow. Roles are a packaging pattern that bundle related tasks, handlers, variables, templates, files, and metadata into a predictable directory layout. That predictability matters when multiple engineers read and reuse automation: a role makes clear where defaults live, where service handlers live, and where templates and static files belong. You will see how using roles improves reuse across projects, reduces duplicated tasks, and helps follow best practices. For example, instead of repeating Nginx installation steps across many playbooks, you create a my_nginx_role once and apply it wherever needed. We will cover the standard role directory, variable precedence between defaults and vars, the notify/handler pattern, and how to scaffold a role with ansible-galaxy init. You will also get a hands-on Nginx role example and common mistakes to avoid, like incorrect template paths or misunderstanding defaults precedence. By the end, you will be able to scaffold a role, populate tasks and handlers, and call that role from a simple playbook to deploy a service reliably. Think about a place where you currently copy-paste tasks — that is the first candidate to convert into a role.

By the end of this chapter you will explain why Ansible roles are essential for organizing automation, describe the standard directory layout for roles, create a new role with ansible-galaxy init, and integrate roles into playbooks. First, you will be able to articulate the benefits: reusability across projects, modularity that splits responsibilities into single-purpose units, and improved readability so teams can find logic quickly. Second, you will recognize the required subdirectories like tasks, handlers, defaults, vars, templates, files, and meta, and explain what each is for with examples. Third, you will scaffold a role using the ansible-galaxy init command to produce consistent files and then populate tasks and handlers. Finally, you will integrate that role into a playbook using the roles keyword and verify the result. Each objective maps to a practical competency: creating a role, placing variables at the correct precedence level, using templates and files correctly, and avoiding common mistakes such as incorrect path references or misunderstanding defaults precedence. These skills matter because production automation must be maintainable, auditable, and reusable across environments.

These objectives map directly to tasks you will perform on an RHCE exam and in real operations work. First, when you design automation for a service like Nginx, you will create a role that installs packages, configures files from a template, and ensures the service is running. Second, you will correctly choose where to put variables: defaults for sensible overrides, vars for internal role settings that rarely change, and inventory group_vars for environment-specific secrets. Third, you will use handlers and notify so configuration changes trigger restarts only when needed. Finally, you will test the role by applying it from a small playbook, and verify service state with common commands. This skillset reduces mistakes during deployments, makes configuration drift easier to detect, and keeps automation portable across environments. A common misconception is that roles are only for large projects; in reality, even a small repeated task benefits from role encapsulation to keep playbooks concise and maintainable.

Roles are an organizational pattern in Ansible that group all artifacts related to a single concern into a predictable structure. That single claim hides important practical consequences. Reusability means you can write a role once, then share it across teams or projects. For example, a role that installs and configures Nginx becomes a single source of truth for that service; you do not copy tasks into every playbook. Modularity helps break large, monolithic playbooks into focused parts: one role for the webserver, another for the database, another for application deployment. This separation reduces cognitive load when you read or debug automation. Maintainability improves because a newcomer can look in the role's defaults, tasks, and templates to find where behavior is defined. Roles also encourage best practices: using defaults for overridable options, using handlers for service restarts, and packaging metadata in meta/main. yml. A common misconception is that roles add unnecessary complexity for small projects. In truth, even small but repeated automation benefits from a role. Begin by identifying repeated task groups — each becomes a good candidate for a role. As a takeaway, treat roles as reusable modules that make automation easier to version, test, and share.

A role follows a predictable directory layout that tells Ansible where to find each type of content. The most common directories are tasks, handlers, defaults, vars, templates, files, meta, and a README. Tasks/main. yml is the entry point executed when the role runs. Handlers/main. yml lists service restart or reload handlers you trigger with notify. Defaults/main. yml holds default values with the lowest precedence; they provide sensible settings users can override. Vars/main. yml contains role-specific high precedence variables used rarely and less likely to be overridden. Templates holds Jinja2 files used with the template module; these allow dynamic configuration by referencing role and inventory variables. Files holds static files to copy with the copy module. Meta/main. yml contains metadata such as author, license, and role dependencies that help composition. This layout matters because Ansible automatically searches these directories for relative src paths, so tasks can refer to a template simply by name. A common mistake is placing a template in the wrong directory or expecting the copy module to look in templates. Use this structure to make role content discoverable and portable.

The tasks/main. yml file is the entry point Ansible reads when a role runs. It is the sequence of steps that implement the role's core behavior. You will often organize this file into includes or blocks to keep it readable, but at its simplest it lists tasks in order: install packages, deploy configuration templates, copy static files, and ensure services are running. Importantly, when a task makes a change to a configuration file, it should notify a handler rather than restart a service immediately. This ensures restarts happen only when necessary. A concrete example: first install the nginx package with the dnf module, then template the nginx configuration and notify "Restart Nginx", then ensure the nginx service is enabled and started. A common mistake is placing idempotent logic in a way that always reports changed, causing unnecessary restarts. Use modules and check options that preserve idempotence. As a quick practice, open tasks/main. yml and write a small sequence: package install, template deploy with notify, service ensure. That pattern will be reused across many roles. tasks/main.yml — Role Entry Point means list the core steps in tasks/main.yml and rely on handlers for reactive operations when changes occur.. In practical terms, how the role executes its tasks and triggers behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Handlers are special tasks that run only when notified by another task during the play. They are typically used to restart or reload services after a configuration change. The core idea is reactive control: a template or file task notifies a named handler when it reports changed, then handlers execute at the end of the role or play to apply required service actions. This reduces noise by ensuring restarts happen only when necessary. A simple flow: a template task writes a new config and reports changed; it sends notify: Restart Nginx; after the current host's tasks finish, Ansible runs the Restart Nginx handler. If multiple tasks notify the same handler, the handler runs just once. Common mistakes include forgetting to notify the handler, which leaves services running old configs, or naming mismatches between notify and handler names. Handlers can be defined inside the role so they are available when the role runs, or in the playbook level for cross-role handlers. Use clear handler names and keep them idempotent. Understanding variable precedence is essential when designing roles. defaults/main. yml contains default variables with the lowest precedence. They are ideal for providing sensible default settings that administrators can override through inventory, group_vars, host_vars, playbook vars, or extra vars. For example, put nginx_port: 80 in defaults so an inventory file can override it for a staging or production environment. Vars/main. yml has higher precedence than defaults; variables here are considered integral to the role and less likely to be overridden. Use vars for values that the role expects to remain constant or that should not be casually changed. A common mistake is placing environment-specific secrets in defaults — those should live in group_vars or be provided via Ansible Vault and inventory. Another pitfall is expecting defaults to block overrides; defaults are intentionally low precedence so they remain easy to override. When writing tasks and templates, reference variables without assuming where they come from, and document overridable settings in the role README. The guiding rule: defaults for flexible settings, vars for role-internal constants, and inventory for environment-specific values. defaults vs vars — Variable Precedence means put adjustable settings in defaults; put role-internal constants in vars; use inventory or vault for environment-specific secrets.. Templates and files are how roles place content on managed hosts. Use the files/ directory for static files that do not require variable substitution, such as a static binary or a default index. html. Use templates/ for Jinja2 templates that render configuration dynamically based on variables. The template module will render templates and place the result on the target host, while the copy module uses files/ for direct copies. A key convenience of roles is that you do not need to specify full paths in src when calling template or copy: Ansible automatically searches the role's templates/ and files/ directories. For example, a template task with src: nginx. conf. j2 will find my_role/templates/nginx. conf. j2. Watch for the common error of putting a template in files/ and then expecting template to render it. Also avoid using absolute local paths which break portability. Use ownership, group, and mode settings in the task to ensure correct permissions. When you need dynamic configurations — for instance, inserting the nginx_port variable into an nginx. conf — templates are the correct choice. There are a few recurring mistakes engineers make when adopting roles. First, variable precedence confusion: placing important environment-specific values in defaults/main. yml means they can be easily overridden, which is correct for tunable settings but wrong for secrets — those should be provided in group_vars, host_vars, or via Ansible Vault. Second, incorrect paths: a common error is using absolute or external paths for src in template or copy tasks. Remember that Ansible looks inside the role's templates/ and files/ directories by default, so use src: nginx. conf. j2 rather than a path to the role directory. Third, forgetting to notify handlers: if a template changes but no notify is present, the service will not reload and configuration changes will be useless until a manual restart. Fourth, always check idempotence — tasks that always report changed will trigger handlers repeatedly and cause unnecessary restarts. When troubleshooting, inspect task output to see which task returned changed and whether handlers were queued. Use smaller test playbooks targeting localhost to iterate quickly. These checks reduce debugging time and prevent unexpected downtime.
